analysis.title: The macroeconomic impact of AI: Higher growth and higher inflation (Economic Insights, 23 October 2026)
key_insights: Global semiconductor sales are just under USD 160 billion per month, more than double a year ago. The growth reflects higher production and sharply rising prices, and is led by integrated circuits and memory. Discrete semiconductors and sensors grow only in single digits.
Asian emerging economies such as South Korea and Taiwan account for more than half of global semiconductor turnover. The US accounts for just over a third.

Semiconductor revenue is expected to grow just under 90% this year, then 27% next year, with further slowdown in 2028 and 2029. The report says the industry would overtake pharmaceuticals and close the gap on autos.

WTO data show trade in AI-linked goods (semiconductors, servers, telecom equipment) rose over 20% last year and made up almost half of global goods trade growth. Trade grew about 5% in 2025 against about 3% a year previously, despite high US tariffs.
Globally, goods trade cannot add growth because exports and imports cancel out. Domestic capital-goods investment (data centres, computer equipment, software) is the potential growth driver.

In the US, investment in computer equipment and software has reached a record 5% of GDP. Investment in data-processing hardware has recently exceeded housing construction. The AI boom masks weakness in other investment areas.

US AI investment accounts for a quarter to a third of economic growth, or 0.5 to 0.7 percentage points on about 2% GDP growth. Only 10% to 20% of computer equipment spending adds value added on balance, because much of the hardware is imported from Asia.
Growth in the current US cycle is mainly driven by private consumption, supported by equity-market wealth gains. Without the AI boom, GDP growth would be significantly lower.

The Fed estimates AI investment adds about 0.4 percentage points to US inflation, mainly through computer equipment costs. Electricity and construction cost effects are smaller but can be large locally where data centres cluster.

US unemployment is around 4% with few new hires and low layoffs. Entry-level jobs and graduate hiring are weaker. IT, financial services and consulting have cut jobs, while health, education, culture and construction add jobs that more than offset the losses.

Europe is largely bypassing the AI boom. The information and communications sector grows about 3% a year against about 1% for the whole economy, contributing only about 0.2 percentage points to GDP growth. Europe has about 5% of global computing capacity against 75% to 80% for the US.
ASML, with a market capitalisation of about EUR 650 billion, is the most valuable company in Europe and the main exception to Europe's lag in advanced chip technology.
The ECB estimates AI could raise European productivity growth by 0.2 to 0.4 percentage points a year in the medium to long term.

Memory chip shortages raised prices of phones, tablets and laptops in Europe, adding about 0.2 percentage points to inflation. Energy prices, up sharply since the war in Iran, account for almost half of the 3.8% inflation rate.
Eurozone unemployment has stayed just over 6% for three years. Swiss unemployment is about 3%, but unemployed graduates in Switzerland have more than doubled in four years.

Demand for semiconductors far exceeds supply and capacity takes years to add. With a four to six year chip lifespan and replacement cycle, the report expects the boom to continue for some time, but with slowing growth.

Asian gains are one-sided. The chip industry is capital-intensive and creates few jobs, and wealth is concentrated among older households with high savings and mortgage burdens, so the boom does not lead to a consumer boom, particularly in South Korea. Taiwan is somewhat better. Growth is K-shaped in both Taiwan and South Korea.

Data centre construction is a temporary growth boost. Building costs are about a quarter of development costs, and electrical and cooling systems are just under half, often imported. Malaysia can benefit longer through ICT service exports as a regional hub.

India is among the biggest potential beneficiaries of generative AI in outsourcing. Physical AI (robotics) favours export-oriented manufacturers such as China, South Korea, Taiwan, Hungary, the Czech Republic and Poland.
China is the only emerging economy able to develop AI models, train them and build end-user applications. It is the only significant competitor to the US in AI.

macro_indicators.interpretation: More than double the level a year ago, helped by sharply higher prices.

risk_factors: Semiconductor growth is expected to level off significantly, with a slowdown in 2027.
AI investment masks weakness in other US investment areas.
AI investment is inflationary in the short run through chip, electricity and construction costs.
Job losses in AI-exposed sectors and weaker entry-level hiring for graduates.
Counting AI investment is imprecise and may overstate its growth effect.
Asian growth is K-shaped and narrow, with limited job creation and consumer spillover.
Europe's low AI adoption and high energy prices limit its participation.

tension_points.bull_case: AI investment adds 0.5 to 0.7 percentage points to US GDP growth, and without it growth would be significantly lower. Semiconductor demand far exceeds supply and the replacement cycle supports the boom.
tension_points.bear_case: Only 10% to 20% of computer equipment spending adds value on balance because of imports, AI investment adds about 0.4 points to inflation, jobs are cut in exposed sectors, and semiconductor growth is expected to level off.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Semiconductor sales growth slowing sharply, as the report expects in 2027 (27% growth versus just under 90% this year).
